deck.headline: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails minutes after launch, destroying all 40 Amazon Leo satellites
deck.sub: The first of 38 Amazon launches ends in ULA's first mission failure; the Pentagon's second rocket is likely grounded.
deck.summary: ULA's Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after launch on 15 Nov, destroying all 40 Amazon Leo satellites on the first of 38 Amazon flights. ULA says it does not yet know why; Ars Technica's sources point to the BE-4-powered booster stage. The rocket is expected to be grounded.
deck.whyItMatters: Vulcan carries about half of the US military's planned national-security launches and most of Amazon's plan to catch Starlink. An indefinite grounding leaves SpaceX, which caught its Starship upper stage a day earlier, even more dominant, and pushes Amazon Leo's rollout back again.
deck.checked: Checked on Ars Technica and The Verge (ULA's and Amazon's statements, time, booster-stage detail) and ULA's own mission page (40 satellites, first of 38 Amazon launches); ULA's failure statement itself was posted on X, which we did not open
deck.storyline: Storyline: who can launch rockets · day 2
deck.detailHtml:
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan lifted off from Cape Canaveral at 12:40 pm EDT on 15 Nov carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites, and failed about 10 minutes into flight; all 40 were lost (Ars Technica, The Verge). ULA said the rocket "suffered an anomaly" and "failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit", that it did not yet have data on the cause, and that "today, we did not meet that standard." Ars Technica's sources say the fault was in the booster stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, not the upper stage or the six solid boosters. The Verge reports it as ULA's first mission failure in 20 years. It was the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has bought; Amazon said ULA has been a trusted partner and it expects ULA to learn from the flight.

Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters, which had failed on two of its four earlier flights, worked this time. The trouble came later: Ars Technica's sources say the core booster stage, powered by two methane-burning BE-4 engines from Blue Origin, had a problem before the 10-minute mark when ULA says the anomaly occurred. ULA has not said what failed and says customers will see the investigation.

The loss matters well beyond one launch. Vulcan is one of two rockets certified for US national-security missions, and Amazon had booked 38 Vulcan flights to build Leo, its Starlink rival, which ULA's mission page says will start with more than 3,000 satellites. Ars expects the rocket to be grounded for an indefinite period while the cause is found.

deck.headline: Bessent wants an outsider to run Nvidia as Huang agrees to testify
deck.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' with an outside CEO and must explain whether chips reached China via shell companies. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify privately to three House committees; Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday.
deck.whyItMatters: Tuesday's results now double as a governance test. Banks and funds with large Nvidia weightings face three risks at once: an outside CEO forced by Washington, tighter export rules, and a possible founder return.
deck.update: Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' from outside and must explain whether it sold to China via shell companies; Huang agrees to testify to three House committees; Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in August 2025; earnings Tuesday.
deck.detailHtml: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shakeup" in leadership and suggested an outside CEO (Bloomberg via Japan Times). He wants answers on whether Nvidia used shell companies to sell chips above the H200 to China: "these shell companies were obvious" (CNA). Rep. John Moolenaar said Jensen Huang has agreed to testify, behind closed doors, to the China select committee and the foreign affairs and intelligence committees, so no subpoenas were issued (BBC). Megaspeed says Alice Huang left on 30 Aug 2025, denies wrongdoing and has hired outside counsel; Singapore says she was still in charge for most of 2025 (TNW). The FT reports Huang is discussing a return; his representative declined to comment. Speaker Mike Johnson sees "growing consensus" on limiting chip exports (The Verge), and The Hill reports scrutiny of Commerce Secretary Lutnick's role. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC News · CNA (AFP): Bessent wants answers · The Japan Times (Bloomberg) · TNW: Megaspeed statement · The Verge: Congress and export rules · Financial Times: Huang discusses comeback · The Hill: scrutiny of Lutnick

deck.headline: Three central banks show FX trades settling across different systems at once
deck.summary: The Bank of England, Singapore's MAS and the Bank of Thailand tested a 'synchronisation' service that settles both legs of FX trades together in central bank money, across both traditional and ledger-based systems, and also netted trades between banks. The BoE plans a live synchronisation interface in 2028.
deck.whyItMatters: FX settlement risk (paying one currency and not receiving the other) is one of the oldest problems in cross-border banking. If synchronisation goes live, treasury and payments teams could settle Asian-currency trades in central bank money without a single shared ledger; watch for the BoE's 2028 interface specification.
deck.checked: Checked on the Bank of England's joint media release (opened); PYMNTS coverage matches
deck.storyline: Storyline: how banks settle across borders · day 1
deck.detailHtml: The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Bank of Thailand published the results of Project Meridian FX APAC on 13 Nov. A prototype synchronisation operator built by Partior coordinated movements of central bank money so that both legs of an FX trade settle together (payment-versus-payment), and also ran multilateral net FX settlement, across test systems that included both real-time gross settlement (RTGS) and distributed-ledger platforms. The banks say it worked across different technologies and time zones, and that netting let banks use liquidity more efficiently. The BoE plans a live synchronisation interface in 2028.

deck.headline: Fireworks AI hack spreads to Uber: drivers' licence data stolen
deck.summary: Uber says hackers stole drivers' personal and licence details from Fireworks AI, an AI inference vendor, after credentials were stolen in October. State filings so far list 7,870 affected people in three states, with more to come. It is the same Fireworks breach behind Cursor's tampered Claude Code extensions.
deck.whyItMatters: A model-hosting vendor turned out to hold identity documents. Banks using third-party inference should ask what customer data their AI vendors keep, for how long, and whether it sits next to credentials attackers can resell.
deck.checked: Checked on TNW (TechCrunch's report, state counts, Fireworks' explanation); Uber's notices themselves not opened
deck.storyline: Storyline: leaked and stolen AI keys and data · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Uber is warning drivers that hackers stole their personal and driver's licence details from a vendor, which TechCrunch identified, and Uber confirmed, as AI inference provider Fireworks AI (via TNW). Uber says Fireworks told it on 9 Oct that internal credentials had been stolen. Notices to state attorneys general list 2,567 people in Massachusetts, 3,430 in South Carolina and 1,873 in Rhode Island, 7,870 so far; California and Illinois residents were notified without a count. Fireworks, valued at $17.5bn in July, has disclosed two October incidents and blames a group that sells stolen access to AI models ("LLMjacking"). It is the same breach Cursor says led to its tampered Claude Code extensions (Developing).
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGTNW (citing TechCrunch) · The Hacker News: Cursor links its incident to Fireworks

deck.headline: South Korea's top tax-exam scorer admits he cheated with a hidden camera and AI
deck.summary: The top scorer in South Korea's tax accountant exam, who got 397.5 of 400, confessed he photographed questions with a hidden camera, sent them to an AI tool and read the answers on a phone. Police are investigating, days before Thursday's national college entrance exam.
deck.whyItMatters: Professional certifications, including banking and accounting exams, rely on proctoring designed before cheap cameras and instant AI answers. Expect device detection, shorter windows and more oral or practical assessment.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI cheating in exams · day 1
deck.detailHtml: The candidate who ranked first in both rounds of South Korea's tax accountant exam in April and July, scoring 397.5 of 400 with one wrong answer out of 160, confessed on 15 Nov that he cheated (The Guardian, Japan Times/AFP). He said he photographed questions with a microcamera, sent them to a generative AI tool and checked answers on a smartphone; he had earlier denied using smart glasses. Seoul police say they received a written confession and assigned investigators. The case lands days before Thursday's national college entrance exam, and education YouTubers are already urging tighter checks or a delay.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Guardian · The Japan Times (AFP) · Reuters (via Google News)

deck.headline: Estonia shuts every Russian border crossing after a GRU-ordered attack on a drone maker
deck.summary: Estonia will close every border crossing with Russia from 1 December after eight people were detained over an attempted arson and bomb attack on drone maker Threod Systems. Estonia's security service says Russia's GRU ordered it; the prime minister links it to support for Ukraine.
deck.whyItMatters: Sabotage against Europe's defence suppliers is moving from warnings to border closures. Firms with Baltic operations or Russian-border logistics should plan for the 1 Dec shutdown.
deck.storyline: Storyline: Russian sabotage in Europe · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, PM Kristen Michal said, after an attempted attack on Threod Systems, which makes long-range attack and reconnaissance drones (The Guardian). Eight people were detained on Saturday; no one was hurt and nothing was damaged. Estonia's internal security service, Kapo, says the attack aimed to cause an explosion and fire and was ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence. Michal tied it to Estonia's support for Ukraine and said the closure sends "a clear message".

deck.headline: Japan's economy unexpectedly shrinks in the third quarter as shoppers pull back
deck.summary: Japan's economy shrank at an annualised 0.1% in July to September, government data showed on Monday, when economists expected 0.3% growth; weak consumer spending was the drag. It complicates the Bank of Japan's rate path as US yields stay high.
deck.whyItMatters: A shrinking economy makes it harder for the Bank of Japan to keep raising rates while US yields sit near 5%; yen and Japanese bank stocks are the ones to watch this week.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the world economy's pace · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Japan's economy contracted an annualised 0.1% in July-September, government data showed on Monday, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth (Reuters via CNA); Reuters and Investing.com headline weaker consumption as the cause. Australian shares also slipped toward a one-week low on weaker copper and iron ore (Mint).

deck.headline: OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra helped prove a step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
deck.summary: OpenAI launched a science blog with a post on how its unreleased GPT-6 Astra helped prove a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model of particle physics. The work, an arXiv paper by physicist Nathaniel Craig, ships with a Lean formalisation; how much Astra contributed is OpenAI's account.
deck.whyItMatters: After maths results in August, this is the first time OpenAI has tied Astra to a frontier physics proof. The claim to check is how much the model contributed versus the author; the Lean files make parts of it checkable.
deck.detailHtml: OpenAI opened a science blog on 15 Nov with a post on how GPT-6 Astra, its unreleased next model, "helped turn the idea into a detailed proof" of a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model (OpenAI's feed summary; the page itself refused our request). The physics is in arXiv paper 2610.09093 by physicist Nathaniel Craig (6 Oct): it builds a gauge-invariant measure for overlap fermions on four-dimensional lattices for chiral gauge theories that include the Standard Model, a long-standing obstacle to simulating the theory from first principles. The paper (123 pages) comes with a Lean formalisation and calculation records.

deck.headline: Old Bitly links in famous tweets were hijacked to send readers elsewhere
deck.summary: Attackers re-pointed old, inactive Bitly links in years-old posts by Burger King, McDonald's, Donald Trump and, per CNN, the FBI and the Defense Department. Bitly confirmed the flaw, suspended the accounts and is disabling the links; some look-alike links still worked late Sunday.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks and regulators have years of shortened links in statements, emails and posts. Each is a phishing path if a shortener lets it be re-pointed; audit old links and prefer your own domain.
deck.storyline: Storyline: hijacked links and web trust · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Old Bitly short links in years-old posts by Burger King, McDonald's and Donald Trump were found redirecting to unrelated pages (Ransomnews), and CNN reports the same for links from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, the FBI and the US Defense Department. Bitly said on X it had found an issue that "allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links", suspended the accounts and is disabling the links. Ransomnews says 49 re-created links that mimic the originals still worked late on 15 Nov.

deck.headline: FDA rejects ivonescimab, the Chinese-born lung cancer drug that once beat Keytruda
deck.summary: The FDA rejected ivonescimab, a lung cancer drug from Summit Therapeutics and China's Akeso, because it slowed tumours but did not help patients live longer. Analysts largely expected it; the decision tests the value of Western licensing deals for Chinese-developed drugs.
deck.whyItMatters: The FDA is holding Chinese-originated drugs to overall-survival evidence, which matters for the many licensing deals Western pharma has struck with Chinese biotechs and for investors pricing them.
deck.detailHtml: The FDA rejected ivonescimab, a lung cancer drug from US biotech Summit Therapeutics and China's Akeso, Summit said on Sunday (STAT). The letter says the drug slowed cancer progression but did not help patients live longer, and that this "does not support the positive benefit-risk profile" needed for approval. Endpoints calls the rejection, in a narrow lung cancer setting, largely expected by analysts.

deck.headline: Iran fires drones at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days
deck.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired six drones at a US radar site at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain, their second attack there in three days; Bahrain says all were shot down. Iran says Hormuz is closed but that a path to a deal remains open.
deck.whyItMatters: Attacks on Gulf hosts of US forces put a floor under oil prices even as the IEA sees a surplus; banks' Gulf exposures and trade-finance desks should watch shipping insurance rates this week.
deck.update: Iran fires six drones at the US radar site at Riffa air base in Bahrain, its second attack in three days; Bahrain says all were intercepted, and Iran's speaker says a path to a deal remains open.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 6
deck.detailHtml: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they launched six drones at the US air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain on Sunday, their second attack on Bahrain in three days (BBC). Bahrain says its air defences destroyed them "before they could achieve their objectives"; sirens sounded nationwide. The IRGC said "the Strait of Hormuz is closed". Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attack (Guardian live). Parliament speaker Ghalibaf said a path to ending the nine-month war is open if the US accepts Iran's "logical conditions"; Trump said he may hold off on strikes absent new provocations (Bloomberg via Japan Times). An Iranian claim that a tanker with 2 million barrels sank in Hormuz (NDTV) is unconfirmed.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC News · The Japan Times (Bloomberg) · The Guardian liveOTHERNDTV: Iran claims tanker sank (unconfirmed)

alsoToday.headline: TSMC confirms leaked employee data came from its cloud provider
alsoToday.summary: TSMC told the SEC that some current and former employees' data was published without authorisation, and that it matches data stored with a cloud service provider; it has found no evidence its own systems were breached (BleepingComputer).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Staff bank details in a public dump mean targeted fraud; banks with TSMC payroll customers in Taiwan should expect impersonation attempts.
alsoToday.detailHtml: TSMC told the SEC that some current and former employees' data was published without authorisation, and that it matches data stored with a cloud service provider; it has found no evidence its own systems were breached (BleepingComputer). A seller called "SmithBianl" had offered a claimed 6.9GB, 46,000-record set including national ID numbers, addresses and banking information, starting at 3 BTC, with a free-leak deadline of 15 Nov.

alsoToday.headline: IDBI Bank unions ask the RBI to hold up Fairfax's Rs 52,878 crore takeover
alsoToday.summary: Two IDBI Bank staff bodies, UFIOE and AIIBEA, asked the RBI on 15 Nov to withhold all approvals for the government's Rs 52,878 crore sale of control of IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings (ETBFSI).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: This is India's first big bank privatisation; how the RBI handles fit-and-proper and funding questions will set the template for future foreign-owned Indian banks.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Two IDBI Bank staff bodies, UFIOE and AIIBEA, asked the RBI on 15 Nov to withhold all approvals for the government's Rs 52,878 crore sale of control of IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings (ETBFSI). They want independent checks on where the money comes from, ultimate ownership, whether IDBI's own deposits or assets could fund the deal, and Fairfax's existing control of CSB Bank. They compare the price with Emirates NBD's purchase of RBL Bank in June and cite IDBI's Rs 3.56 lakh crore of deposits.

alsoToday.headline: Starling's founder is building Lockwood, a bank designed for AI agents
alsoToday.summary: Anne Boden, who founded Starling, is building Lockwood, a bank she says will be "built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents" (Sunday Times interview, reported by Sifted and Dealroom).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Agent spending limits are becoming a product, not just a risk control (see ChatGPT Wallet and Wells Fargo's new terms). Incumbent banks will need per-agent mandates of their own.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: AI agents and financial firms · day 5
alsoToday.detailHtml: Anne Boden, who founded Starling, is building Lockwood, a bank she says will be "built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents" (Sunday Times interview, reported by Sifted and Dealroom). Customers would give each AI agent a spending limit, for example a £100 monthly grocery cap for a shopping assistant, and Lockwood would refuse anything outside it. It will offer a current account only, no loans or savings, start with an e-money licence in 2027 and become a bank in 2028. Boden is funding it herself for now and targets a million customers in year one.
alsoToday.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGSifted (via Google News)AGGREGATORDealroom news note

alsoToday.headline: Zelensky urges the US and Musk to lift Starshield limits before winter
alsoToday.summary: President Zelensky says Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service Ukraine uses to intercept missiles and drones, is still restricted and too slow, and that protecting the energy grid this winter "directly depends" on lifting the limits (BBC).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A private satellite network is now a lever in a war and in peace talks, ahead of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting on 19 Nov.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: talks to end the Ukraine war · day 5
alsoToday.detailHtml: President Zelensky says Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service Ukraine uses to intercept missiles and drones, is still restricted and too slow, and that protecting the energy grid this winter "directly depends" on lifting the limits (BBC). He urged the US and Elon Musk to be "on the right side of history". The slowdown was first noticed in October; Musk has said the US government controls Starshield, while Trump said he told Musk to "put it back". It follows Zelensky's claim that the US floated Donbas-for-NATO (15 Nov).

alsoToday.headline: Pentagon renames its AI office the 'Super Intelligence Office'
alsoToday.summary: The Pentagon (now styled the Department of War) renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office the Super Intelligence Office on Friday (SecurityWeek). Cameron Stanley, a former Project Maven lead, is now Chief Super Intelligence Officer; programmes including the Maven Smart System targeting platform continue, and resources move to SI.mil.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A rename, not new money, but contract language and vendor paperwork for US government AI work will start to change.
alsoToday.detailHtml: The Pentagon (now styled the Department of War) renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office the Super Intelligence Office on Friday (SecurityWeek). Cameron Stanley, a former Project Maven lead, is now Chief Super Intelligence Officer; programmes including the Maven Smart System targeting platform continue, and resources move to SI.mil. It follows Trump's September executive order 14434 telling agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead of AI where the law allows.

alsoToday.headline: Apple plans to show Siri smart glasses at WWDC and ship them by end-2027, Bloomberg says
alsoToday.summary: Apple plans to unveil smart glasses at its next WWDC and ship them by the end of 2027, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports (via 9to5Mac). They will not run apps themselves but lean on a nearby iPhone, with Wi-Fi as a fallback, and Apple is laying groundwork for third-party apps in Siri from the iOS 27.3 beta.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Apple joins Meta and Google-Samsung (shipping 10 Dec) in AI glasses; a camera on every face raises the same bystander-privacy questions banks face for branch and trading-floor policies.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: AI glasses and wearables · day 2
alsoToday.detailHtml: Apple plans to unveil smart glasses at its next WWDC and ship them by the end of 2027, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports (via 9to5Mac). They will not run apps themselves but lean on a nearby iPhone, with Wi-Fi as a fallback, and Apple is laying groundwork for third-party apps in Siri from the iOS 27.3 beta. Test units are slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans, with flush cameras and a use indicator light.

alsoToday.headline: Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins the WTA Finals on her debut
alsoToday.summary: Mirra Andreeva, 19, beat Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at her first attempt, having also beaten her in the group stage (The Athletic). Svitolina had knocked out Aryna Sabalenka in the semi-finals.

alsoToday.headline: US flight cancellations ease to about 1,900 on day three after the FAA stop
alsoToday.summary: US airlines cancelled nearly 1,900 flights and delayed more than 6,300 by mid-afternoon on Sunday, after more than 6,600 cancellations on Saturday, as they recovered from Friday's four-hour nationwide ground stop (Bloomberg via Japan Times, citing FlightAware).
alsoToday.update: Disruption eases: about 1,900 US flights cancelled on Sunday after 6,600+ on Saturday, as the FAA investigates the faulty router.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: when air traffic systems fail · day 3
alsoToday.detailHtml: US airlines cancelled nearly 1,900 flights and delayed more than 6,300 by mid-afternoon on Sunday, after more than 6,600 cancellations on Saturday, as they recovered from Friday's four-hour nationwide ground stop (Bloomberg via Japan Times, citing FlightAware). American had the most cancellations (613) and JetBlue cut more than a quarter of its schedule. The FAA is still investigating the router installed during a copper-to-fibre upgrade.
